title: Ebola Workers Evacuated From Congo Hospital After Three Days Trapped by Fighting in Ituri
summary: About a dozen Ebola response workers, including WHO staff, were evacuated from a hospital in Akwe after three days sheltering from heavy fighting between the Congolese army and the CRP rebel group, as the country's deadliest Ebola outbreak on record reaches nearly 12,000 cases.
content:
Ebola response workers trapped for three days by heavy fighting in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo have been evacuated to safety, the World Health Organization said on Tuesday, in a rescue that underlines how war is now the biggest obstacle to containing the country's worst Ebola outbreak on record.

About a dozen people, including two WHO staff members and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, after spending three full days sheltering inside a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire. United Nations peacekeepers helped carry out the evacuation, deploying a mobile operating base and reinforcing patrols around Akwe and neighbouring villages, according to Reuters.

"They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them," Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO's Ebola incident manager, told the Associated Press.

The workers had been forced to take cover in the hospital's maternity ward as clashes raged around them. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Sunday that agency staff and Ebola responders had been sheltering "for their lives" and called for their "immediate safe passage and for the hospital facilities, staff and patients to be protected", according to UN News.

The fighting pits the Congolese army against the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP), a rebel group led by Thomas Lubanga, and has intensified since the weekend in Djugu territory, one of the epicentres of the outbreak. At least 10 people have been killed in the clashes, UN News reported, and the rebel advance toward Bunia has raised fears of a wider escalation. Thousands of civilians have fled their homes, and the United Nations has temporarily restricted staff movements in parts of Djugu, according to Xinhua.

The WHO has also temporarily relocated its Ebola response team and partner staff from Mongbwalu, one of the original epicentres of the outbreak, after fighting disrupted road access. Personnel from both the WHO and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention were evacuated from Mongbwalu to Bunia on Tuesday, Xinhua reported, citing local media.

The disruption is already being felt across the response. Fighting has prevented teams from reaching some communities, interrupted the monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centres short of staff, Smallwood said. It is the latest blow to an operation that health officials have repeatedly warned is being undermined by insecurity as much as by the virus itself.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus, was declared on 15 May and has since sickened 11,762 people and killed 5,775 across 68 health zones in eight provinces, according to figures released by the WHO on 20 November. Reuters, citing more recent government data, put the toll higher still, at 11,955 cases and 5,867 deaths. Either way, it is the deadliest Ebola outbreak the country has ever recorded.

Ituri remains the hardest-hit province, with more than 8,000 confirmed cases and 3,791 deaths, a case fatality rate of 47 percent, according to the WHO. The province accounts for more than two-thirds of all confirmed cases in the country.

The violence is not new to the response, but it is getting worse. Since 1 January, the WHO has verified more than 87 attacks on healthcare in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, UN News reported, and the agency has warned repeatedly that attacks on civilians and health workers are among the main obstacles to containing the virus.

There was one piece of encouraging news this week. Gavi, the global vaccine alliance, announced that it intends to purchase up to 1.5 million doses of a candidate vaccine against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus, a step that could eventually give responders a new tool if the vaccine proves effective and reaches the field.

For now, though, the immediate priority is keeping the response alive in territory where the fighting is spreading. The evacuation from Akwe succeeded, but with teams pulled back from Mongbwalu, roads closed and contacts going unmonitored, health officials fear the virus will exploit the gap. The WHO has said it will keep working with local health authorities and humanitarian partners to restore access, but as Smallwood's account makes clear, that depends on a pause in fighting that neither side has offered.

The events in Ituri are a reminder that the Ebola emergency in Congo is now two crises at once: an epidemic that has already killed nearly 6,000 people, and a war that keeps the people fighting it from reaching the patients who need them.
